lesson.title: When Answers Aren't the Truth: Understanding Response Bias
lesson.summary: Response bias is the distortion that appears in survey data because respondents shade, hide, or misremember the truth, even when the sample itself is perfectly chosen.
lesson.body:
Response bias is the distortion that creeps into survey data not because of who was asked, but because of how the people who were asked chose to answer. A survey can start with a flawless simple random sample and still produce numbers that are quietly wrong, because respondents shade the truth, misremember, or simply tell the interviewer what they think the interviewer wants to hear. This is a different failure mode than bias caused by an incomplete sampling frame or by people refusing to respond at all: those problems change who ends up in the data, while response bias changes what the people already in the data actually say.

Several forces push respondents away from the truth. Social desirability makes people overreport good behaviors like voting or exercising and underreport bad ones like drug use or cheating. Sensitive or embarrassing topics trigger defensive answers. The identity of the interviewer can matter too, since people sometimes give different answers about race relations to an interviewer of a different race than to one of their own. Even memory plays a role, since people asked how many times they visited a doctor last year tend to round, guess, or simply forget.

Because response bias comes from the respondent's incentive to misrepresent the truth, the fix usually involves changing that incentive rather than changing the sample. Anonymous, self administered surveys typically get more honest answers on sensitive topics than face to face interviews. One especially elegant fix is the randomized response technique, developed by the statistician Stanley Warner in 1965, which lets a researcher estimate the true proportion of people who did something sensitive without ever learning any individual respondent's real answer.

Here is how it works, with numbers. Suppose a researcher wants to estimate what proportion of students have ever cheated on an exam, a question few students would answer honestly if asked directly. Each student privately flips a coin. If it lands heads, probability 0.5, the student answers the sensitive question truthfully. If it lands tails, probability 0.5, the student instead answers a harmless, unrelated question with a known probability of yes, such as whether they were born in the first half of the year, where P(yes) is about 0.5. The researcher never learns which question a given student answered, only the final yes or no. If p represents the true proportion of cheaters, the overall probability of a yes response combines both paths: P(yes) = 0.5 times p, plus 0.5 times 0.5. If 40 percent of students said yes overall, then 0.40 = 0.5p + 0.25, which gives 0.5p = 0.15 and p = 0.30. The researcher can now report that roughly 30 percent of students have cheated, even though no single answer ever revealed which question any one student actually answered.

This technique will not appear on every survey you design, but it illustrates the core idea behind fighting response bias: honesty improves when respondents feel protected, and a well designed survey process can extract accurate population level information even when individuals have strong reasons to lie. The next chapter turns to a subtler and more common source of the same problem, one that shows up in almost every survey ever written: the exact wording of the question itself.
